title: Police seek public assistance in identifying fraud suspects
summary: We are asking for the public's help to identify a man and a woman who are believed to be responsible for fraudulently using Apple Pay accounts earlier this year. A Calgary woman noticed suspicious activity on her Apple Pay account, including 15 unauthorized transactions totalling more than $5,000, made in July 2026. The woman reported the fraudulent activity to police who began investigating. Officers determined the suspects entered various local retail stores and used the tap method of payment on a cellphone to complete several fraudulent transactions. After exhausting all investigative avenues to identify the suspects, police are turning to the public for their help in hopes of advancing the investigation. The first suspect is described as a man wearing a black ball cap with a yellow marking on the peak, sunglasses positioned on the cap, dark clothing, and brown or green pants with black patches. The second suspect is described as a woman with shoulder-length dark hair, wearing a pink shirt, blue jeans and white runners. She was also observed wearing a light-green jacket while committing some of the offences. Anyone with information about the identity of the suspects is asked to contact police by calling 403-266-1234. title: The City releases proposed 2027–2030 Budget focused on Calgarians' priorities
summary: Today, The City of Calgary released its proposed 2027–2030 Budget, outlining how The City plans to deliver services Calgarians rely on while responding to the needs of a growing city. The proposed four-year budget focuses on the priorities of Calgarians and Council, value for tax dollars and maintaining reliable services. Affordability remains an important concern for Calgarians, alongside the need to invest in required services and infrastructure as Calgary continues to grow. The budget takes a balanced approach to these pressures through thoughtful investment in services, critical infrastructure and Calgary's long-term needs. “Calgarians expect reliable services today and a city that is prepared for tomorrow,” said David Duckworth, Chief Administrative Officer. “We know affordability is important to Calgarians, and we also need to continue investing in the services and infrastructure that support a growing city. This budget is about balancing those pressures and making thoughtful choices that maintain the services Calgarians rely on today while preparing our city for the future.” For Calgarians, that means proposed investments that: Maintain reliable services and infrastructure: $1.7 billion: Upgrade the Pine Creek and Fish Creek wastewater treatment plants and invest an additional $616 million in water infrastructure to support reliable service and growth through the North and South Water Feedermains. $420 million: Rehabilitate pavement to extend the life of Calgary's roads. $284 million: Invest in places where Calgarians gather, play and stay active through GamePLAN, including the Forest Lawn recreation facility replacement, Kingsland and Belmont athletic parks and The City's portion of the Foothills Fieldhouse. $66 million: Maintain arenas, aquatic centres and the Calgary Soccer Centre to ensure access to recreation facilities across the city. Support safety and safe communities: $192 million: Provide Calgary Police Service with the facilities, vehicles, equipment and tools needed to serve communities. $102 million: Build new fire and emergency response stations — including facilities serving the downtown and Keystone areas — to help crews respond when Calgarians need them. $94 million: Improve safety for people walking, wheeling, cycling and driving through the Mobility Safety and Speed Management Program. Keep Calgary moving through transit and transportation: $300 million: Purchase buses to support RouteAhead and maintain dependable transit service as Calgary grows. $142 million: Build the 194th Avenue and Macleod Trail interchange to improve connections and traffic flow in south Calgary. $71 million: Advance the Blue Line LRT extension from Saddletowne to 88 Avenue N.E. to improve transit access in northeast Calgary. Accommodate growth and evolving neighbourhoods: $59 million: Renew Village Square Leisure Centre so it can continue to provide recreation opportunities and serve northeast communities. $47 million: Redevelop the Forest Lawn Civic Centre to support City services and community activity in east Calgary. For a full list of investments, visit calgary.ca/budget. The proposed budget includes $6 billion in operating expenditures in 2027 and $21 billion in recommended capital over four years, including $13 billion in new capital infrastructure. In 2027, it requires a 15 per cent increase in municipal property tax revenue from existing properties. For a typical single residential property, the estimated bill impact is an additional $37 per month for municipal property tax and $16 per month for water, waste and recycling, for a combined increase of about $53 per month. Individual impacts will vary based on property assessment and service use. “Calgarians have been clear that they want a safer city, reliable services and infrastructure that keeps up with our growth,” said Mayor Jeromy Farkas. “They also want us to respect how hard they're working to make ends meet. This proposed budget is the starting point, not the final word. Council has some tough decisions ahead. We will be going through the numbers carefully, challenging assumptions and looking for savings. My priority is to protect the services Calgarians count on and address the infrastructure that has been neglected for too long. We need to make every dollar count.” Next steps in the budget process Starting today, Calgarians can submit written comments or register to speak at Council as part of the Public Submissions process. Public Submissions begin Nov. 23, giving Calgarians another opportunity to provide input directly to Council before final decisions are made. Council will begin deliberations on the proposed 2027–2030 Budget the week of Nov. 23, with final approval following debate. View the proposed budget and have your say at calgary.ca/budget. -30-

title: Police search for witnesses to violent assault

title: Calgary Fire Crews Respond to Basement Fire in Community of Dover
summary: Just before 4 am this morning, Calgary Fire Department (CFD) crews responded to reports of a house fire in the 100 block of Doverthorn Close SE. Upon arrival, fire crews noticed smoke showing from a single-family bungalow and quickly gained access and extended hand lines to control and knock down the fire and search the home. One resident from the home self-evacuated and was assessed by EMS. Fire crews rescued two residents from the basement and transferred patient care to EMS after exiting the home. One cat is deceased. Crews remain on scene and are ventilating the structure, checking for any fire extension, and ensuring the fire is out. A fire investigator is also on scene conducting an investigation to determine the cause of the fire. Calgary Fire would like to remind people that working smoke alarms save lives. Test your smoke alarms monthly, change the battery annually and replace smoke alarms when they reach 10 years of age. For more information on fire prevention and fire safety, please visit www.calgary.ca/fire -30-

title: Charge laid in 2006 cold case sexual assault
summary: Twenty years after an aggravated sexual assault in the community of Forest Heights, we have identified and charged a suspect in connection with the case. On Sunday, Aug. 6, 2006, at approximately 4:30 a.m., an 18-year-old woman was walking through a school field in the 500 block of 47 Street S.E., when she was attacked by a male riding a bicycle. During the attack, the victim was sexually assaulted and stabbed multiple times. Evidence collected during the investigation was submitted to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) for forensic testing, and a DNA profile believed to belong to the offender was entered into the National DNA Data Bank in 2006. Over the past two decades, investigators pursued numerous avenues to identify the person responsible, including public appeals, while continuing to review the case as investigative techniques and technology evolved. On Monday, Sept. 21, 2026, investigators were notified of a DNA match through the National DNA Data Bank, linking DNA obtained in 2006 to an individual currently incarcerated for unrelated offences. As a result, we have charged the accused, who was 14 years old at the time of the offence, with one count of aggravated sexual assault. Because he was a youth at the time, he cannot be named under the provisions of the Youth Criminal Justice Act. He will next appear in court on Friday, Dec. 18, 2026. "We never stop pursuing answers for victims of sexual assault, no matter how much time has passed," says Staff Sgt. Tom Hanson of the Calgary Police Service Sexual Assault Investigative Unit. "This case was moved forward by the persistence of many investigators, from those who began the investigation in 2006 to those who saw it through to a charge. Unsolved doesn't mean forgotten." In Canada, there is no time limit on reporting a sexual assault. Anyone who believes they are a victim of sexual assault is encouraged to report it, even if many years have passed since the incident. Anyone with information about this incident, or similar incidents, is asked to contact police by calling 403-266-1234. title: Calgary Fire Responds to 17th Avenue SE Fire
summary: At around 7:15pm on Sunday November 8, fire crews responded to the 4900 block of 17 Avenue SE for a structure fire. Calgary 9-1-1 reported multiple callers as crews arrived at a single-story strip mall complex with heavy smoke and flames showing along the exterior of the building. Firefighters stretched hose lines and began knocking back the fire as heavy winds rapidly spread fire into the roof and further along the structure. Enmax was called to shut off power to the overhead powerlines, before firefighters could safely access the roof, as fire had spread to a power pole and overhead lines connected to the building's roof. Once safe, ladder trucks were set up to access the roof, where firefighters cut a trench to prevent the further spread of fire. Crews forced entry to several adjacent units to check for fire extension and there were no injuries reported. The fire spread rapidly throughout the structure and heavy winds contributed to re-ignition of hot spots. The building is heavily damaged and several businesses are impacted. Fire watch crews were assigned overnight. Calgary Fire Investigators were on scene this morning and Calgary Police Service is assisting with the investigation. Investigators have confirmed the fire originated on the exterior of the building and are working to determine the cause. -30-

title: City of Calgary ready for the winter season
summary: As Calgary prepares for the return of winter weather, The City is ready to respond with crews, equipment and a Council-approved priority snow plan designed to keep people moving safely. New high-capacity snow-clearing equipment has been added to the fleet this season, helping crews clear high-priority roadways and support efficient winter maintenance operations. “Calgarians can be assured that crews and contractors are ready 24 hours a day, seven days a week throughout the winter,” said Chris Hewitt, Manager of Mobility Maintenance. “The City of Calgary is continually exploring ways to improve winter maintenance operations. This year, we will trial a new wing plow that can clear multiple lanes in a single pass, allowing crews to clear roads more efficiently and helping Calgarians get where they need to go safely after a snowfall." Following a snowfall, the snow clock officially begins. Crews focus on following our Council approved Priority Snow Plan , outlined in the City's Winter Maintenance policy. Calgary's busiest routes are cleared first, including roads such as Glenmore Trail, Macleod Trail and Memorial Drive, along with City-owned sidewalks, priority pathways and pedestrian overpasses. Major transit and residential routes are our next priority as crews continue to work through the snow clearing priority network. “Now is the time for Calgarians to prepare for changing conditions as we expect winter weather ahead,” said Hewitt. “When snow arrives, slow down, leave extra space between vehicles and give snow-clearing equipment plenty of room to work.” Calgarians should also ensure their vehicles are winter-ready, with topped-up fluids, a brush or scraper, and have an emergency kit on hand. Before travelling, clear snow from your vehicle and dress appropriately for the conditions whether you're walking, wheeling, cycling or driving. For more information on the City's winter maintenance program, please visit: · Calgary.ca/snow , · Follow along with our plows on our road conditions map , · Learn more about sidewalk shoveling responsibilities .

title: Shop local, share the joy: Mayor highlights 2026 Support Local Holiday campaign in Bowness and Montgomery
summary: As the holiday season approaches, Mayor Jeromy Farkas visited Bowness and Montgomery to kick off the 2026 Support Local Holiday campaign, encouraging Calgarians to shop local and show some love to the businesses that make our neighbourhoods special. Now in its eighth year, the campaign reflects The City's ongoing commitment to supporting local business community. “The holidays are about connection, and some of the most meaningful connections happen right in our own neighbourhoods,” said Mayor Jeromy Farkas. “Calgary is built on the hard work, determination and dreams of people who believe in what they do. More than nine in ten businesses in our city are small businesses, and behind them are our neighbours, friends and families who help make Calgary feel like home. This holiday season, let's show up for them because a little local love goes a long way.” Throughout 2026, City teams and community partners worked together on initiatives that helped Calgarians explore their neighbourhoods, discover local businesses and enjoy experiences close to home. Highlights include: Bringing fresh, local food closer to home : The Farm Stand Program connected Calgarians with local and regional producers through 29 farm stands operated by seven different farmers at community associations, parks and transit-accessible locations across the city. From May 1 to Oct. 14, the Farm Stand webpage was viewed more than 26,000 times, reflecting strong interest in fresh, seasonal produce and local growers. Making downtown a year-round destination : From summer festivals and lively patios to winter markets and holiday celebrations, downtown Calgary offers plenty of reasons to explore, shop and dine local. The Downtown Summer campaign highlighted festivals, attractions, restaurants and shops, helping residents and visitors discover what Calgary has to offer. International visitor spending increased 15.6 per cent year over year, including a 12.2 per cent rise in overseas visitor spending, contributing to Calgary's economy. As winter approaches, the Chill Downtown this Winter Campaign will be in market from Nov.16, 2026 to March 31, 2027 and will feature monthly custom itineraries to entice Calgarians and visitors to come downtown during the winter months at www.exploredowntownyyc.com. Bringing culture and connection to winter: Through Calgary's Winter City Strategy and signature events like New Year's Eve and Chinook Blast, The City is helping create vibrant winter experiences that bring people together and support local businesses, artists and creators. Making public spaces more welcoming in winter also create economic, social and cultural opportunities while helping Calgary grow as a world-renowned winter destination. Explore winter events, activities and initiatives here. Promoting local businesses with BIAs : The City partners with Calgary's 15 Business Improvement Areas (BIAs) to support local businesses, share events and help Calgarians discover the energy, creativity and local business spirit of our BIAs. Learn more about upcoming BIA Winter Events across the city. Encouraging local shopping through the Winter Parking Contest : From November 4 to December 22, Calgary Parking's citywide Winter Parking Contest will encourage Calgarians to discover, celebrate and support local businesses throughout the winter season. Participants can recommend a favourite local business for a chance to win one of seven weekly $150 parking-credit prizes. The campaign will also share practical parking and access information to help Calgarians plan winter outings and explore businesses, destinations and seasonal experiences across the city. “After eight years of Support Local, the passion and determination of Calgary's small business owners remain unchanged,” said Erin Chrusch, Leader of The City's Business & Local Economy team. “We know many businesses continue to face challenges, and that's why support matters more than ever. By working together with Calgarians, City teams, BIAs and community partners, we're helping local businesses stay visible, connected and supported throughout the year. Whether it's a coffee, a gift or a recommendation, even the smallest choices can make a meaningful difference.” “Mainstreet Bowness is exceptional for holiday shopping because we have more than 60 independent local businesses, with something for everyone, from specialty grocery stores to creative studios and local makers,” said Kellie Freeman, Executive Director of Mainstreet Bowness BIA . “We also have a great small-town vibe, with lots of historic buildings and long-standing businesses. We hope everyone comes out to support local artisans, explore Mainstreet Bowness and enjoy our festive community markets starting with our Holiday craft fair this weekend.” Jessica Lapuz, Executive Director of the Montgomery BIA added: “Montgomery has great main street charm right on the banks of the Bow River. This winter we're kicking off the season at Light Up Montgomery on Saturday, Nov. 14, from 5 to 8 p.m. at Montgomery Town Square, and we welcome everyone to eat, shop and enjoy the outdoors with our vibrant mix of more than 115 businesses.” Calgarians are encouraged to explore their neighbourhoods, discover local shops and restaurants, and keep supporting Calgary businesses into the new year. Learn more about the Support Local campaign at calgary.ca/supportlocal. For tools and resources to support business, visit Business and local economy.

title: Fifth Safer Calgary – Operation Order continues coordinated response to crime and social disorder
summary: On Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, we continued our efforts to address crime and social disorder in Calgary through our fifth Operation Order. Throughout the day, Calgary Police Service officers worked alongside Calgary Community Safety, Transit Public Safety, the Alberta Sheriffs, Emergency Health Services Alberta, and community agencies to enforce laws and bylaws, execute outstanding warrants, engage with businesses and community members and connect individuals with services and supports. “There is no single police operation that will solve the complex challenges we are seeing in our city, but stepping back and simply accepting crime and social disorder is not an option,” says Chief Katie McLellan. “When enforcement is necessary, we will take action. When there is an opportunity to connect someone with supports that can help move them toward greater stability, we will do that as well. We will continue working with our partners to find the most effective ways to address these concerns and make Calgary safer.” “Calgarians deserve to feel safe in the communities and public spaces they use every day,” says Mike Ellis, Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Services. “Operations like these, led by the Calgary Police Service, with support from Alberta Sheriffs and other partners, demonstrate the importance of working together to address crime and social disorder, while also connecting people with the services and supports they need.” “Public safety is fundamental to a strong and vibrant city,” says Mayor Jeromy Farkas. “Through Safer Calgary – Operation Order, we are seeing police, city, provincial and community partners working side-by-side to address the concerns Calgarians are experiencing in their communities. These ongoing, coordinated efforts are an important part of keeping Calgary safe for everyone.” Operation Order results The numbers below reflect totals from the CPS enforcement actions throughout the operation. Calls attended: 320 Persons charged: 10 Charges laid: 18 Summonses issued: 99 Arrest warrants executed: 170 Proactive community engagements: 330 Social support and outreach referrals: 165 Operation Order highlights In the East Village, CPS members arrested two people in connection with a robbery and possession of illegal cigarettes. One was also found to be in breach of probation. The individuals were taken into custody and charged. CPS members connected a woman who is seven months pregnant and in need of housing with one of the beds reserved for CPS referrals at the Navigation Centre, ensuring she will have a place to stay while she works to access further supports and longer-term housing. During a proactive patrol at the City Hall CTrain station, Transit peace officers recognized a person matching a missing person report recently shared by the RCMP. Officers detained the individual for a bylaw offence and determined they also had outstanding warrants. CPS members encountered an illegal cigarette sale in the downtown west end, resulting in the seizure of 44 cartons containing more than 8,000 cigarettes. Along with enforcement under Alberta's Tobacco Tax Act, the suspect was referred to Community Court. CPS members patrolling the Beltline witnessed an assault in progress and intervened. Two individuals were arrested and charged with assault. Operation Order is part of our broader approach to public safety and has been complemented by more sustained initiatives, including Safer Calgary – Operation CERTainty and the recently concluded Operation Restore. Each initiative is designed to address public safety concerns through different levels of focused and sustained activity. More information about our ongoing Safer Calgary work is available on the Creating Safe Public Spaces page on the Calgary Police Service website.

title: Calgary Fire Department Responds to Montgomery Garage Fire
summary: Just before 10:00am, fire crews responded to the 2300 block of Mackay Road NW for a structure fire. Crews arrived to find heavy flames and smoke coming from a detached garage at the rear of a single-story residential property. Firefighters stretched a high-volume hose line into the alley and began knocking down the fire in the garage. A second hose line was stretched into the back yard to prevent the spread of fire to the home. Occupants from the neighbouring homes had all self-exited and no injuries were reported. The home was considered vacant, with windows and doorways boarded up and utilities previously disconnected. The fire was contained to the garage and stopped from spreading to the home and neighbouring homes. The garage sustained severe structural damage. A fire investigator attended the scene, and the cause remains under investigation. A fire watch crew has been assigned to monitor conditions. The Calgary Fire Department is part of the Coordinated Safety Response Team (CSRT), working with agencies such as the Calgary Police Service, Alberta Health Services and other City services to address vacant and problem properties that may pose safety risks to occupants, neighbouring properties and the surrounding community. By bringing multiple agencies together, the team works to address complex safety concerns and reduce community risk. Calgarians who are concerned about a vacant or problem property can report their concerns through Calgary 311 . When making a report, provide the property address or location, a description of the concern, when the issue was observed and photos, if they can be taken safely. This information helps City staff assess the concern and direct it to the appropriate service. Do not enter a property or put yourself at risk to gather information. If there is an emergency or immediate threat to life or safety, call 911. -30-

title: Sport Hub coach named captain of Canada's national cricket team: bringing international experience to Calgary kids and teens
summary: Every young person's journey in sport starts with an opportunity to play. A great coach can turn a rocky first try into a positive experience, helping a young person build the confidence, skills and love for sport that keeps them coming back. This is the kind of experience that The City of Calgary's Sport Hub program aims to create by connecting kids and teens in Calgary with qualified coaches from local sport organizations. One of those coaches is Hamza Tariq, who this fall reached a major milestone in his own sport journey when he was named captain of the Canadian national cricket team. Hamza also coaches with Sport Hub through Future Cricket Stars Academy, helping introduce the next generation to cricket. For kids and teens trying the sport, it's an opportunity to learn from someone who understands the game from grassroots participation to international competition. Making the first try count Through Sport Hub, Calgary kids and teens can experience different sports and other recreation activities led by qualified coaches from sport organizations. By bringing the program into schools and communities, providing equipment and offering free or low-cost community lessons, Sport Hub helps reduce barriers to participation and makes it easier for more young people to get involved. But getting the opportunity to try is only the first step. What happens once a young person gets there matters too. “A child's first experience with a sport can shape whether they want to keep playing,” said Brett Whittingham, Recreation Programs Leader. “That's why the coaches delivering Sport Hub programs matter. We want kids learning from people who know the sport and can make that first experience a positive one.” “The impact of quality coaching is immense and I think it's a non-negotiable,” Hamza said. A knowledgeable coach can meet young people where they're at, helping them learn new skills, build confidence and feel comfortable trying, even when they don't get it right the first time. Hamza has seen that change firsthand. Participants who are hesitant to join in on the first day can become more engaged as the program progresses. “We can visibly see the difference in a kid from day one to day five,” he said. For him, a positive experience doesn't depend on how skilled a participant becomes. He remembers Sport Hub participants who struggled with some of the skills but finished the program telling coaches, “This was the best week of my life.” From a first try to what comes next Years ago, while coaching cricket as part of the Sport Hub pilot at Crossing Park School in Martindale, Hamza saw how invested students became in the sport. One young participant approached him after the program with a question: “What do we do afterwards? How do I continue playing?” That question stayed with Hamza. By working with local sport organizations, Sport Hub helps introduce kids and teens to different sports while connecting them with organizations that can help them continue to play. The goal isn't to turn every Sport Hub participant into an elite athlete. It's to develop skills and physical literacy, have fun and enjoy an experience, rather than a competition. With knowledgeable coaches leading the way, young people can have a positive first experience that gives them a reason to keep playing. For some, that might mean finding a new hobby, building confidence or making new friends. For others, it could be the beginning of a lifelong connection to sport, whether as an athlete, coach or community leader. For Hamza, that's what makes returning to Sport Hub feel “full circle.” The teenager who once discovered a love for cricket is now using his experience to help young people find their own reasons to keep playing. Every kid and teen deserves a chance to play. Learn more about Sport Hub and how to get involved at calgary.ca/SportHub . -30-

title: Water Restrictions in effect as Calgary enters home stretch of feeder main work
summary: City-wide Stage 4 water restrictions are in effect as crews begin work to connect the new Bearspaw South Feeder Main to the City water system. This is one of the final steps before the new pipe is complete. The restrictions are expected to last approximately four weeks. Once the pipe is connected, we will need to fill, flush, and conduct water quality testing before the pipe is put into service in December. Calgarians, along with our neighbours in Airdrie, Chestermere, Strathmore and Tsuut'ina Nation are asked to help reduce water use by: Not using water outdoors, including no outdoor flooding of skating rinks. Running dishwashers and washing machines only with full loads. Flushing toilets only when needed. Taking shorter showers, aiming for three minutes or less. Water restrictions apply to all residents and businesses. We're also asking everyone to help spread the word with family, friends, coworkers, and neighbours. Why restrictions are needed To safely connect the new pipe to our water system, the existing feeder main must be temporarily shut down, significantly reducing the amount of water that can be distributed across Calgary and the region. During this time, The City will rely primarily on the Glenmore Water Treatment Plant to supply water to everyone. To maintain reliable water service, ensuring we have enough water for fighting fires and keeping the water system working well, water demand needs to stay below 500 million litres per day. Staying at or below this target will help keep Calgary out of the “risky red zone,” where demand could affect our ability to provide the water service Calgary and the region count on every day. “We're in the home stretch of installing and connecting this pipe, and we're confident Calgarians and the region will step up and reduce their water use again,” says Michael Thompson, Chief Operating Officer of The City of Calgary Water Utility. "Every water-saving action adds up to big savings and helps ensure our water system can continue providing the essential services we rely on.” The City will provide daily updates on water demand and how it is tracking against the 500 million litre target. Water saving tips and the latest information can be found at calgary.ca/savewater .

title: Calgary Police Service announces co-location partnership with YWCA Calgary and FearIsNotLove
summary: The Calgary Police Service (CPS) Domestic Conflict Unit (DCU) has partnered with YWCA Calgary and FearIsNotLove to launch a new co-location model designed to strengthen support for individuals and families impacted by family violence. The partnership comes as family violence continues to affect thousands of Calgarians each year, with CPS responding to an average of 2,076 domestic related calls for service each month. The announcement coincides with Family Violence Prevention Month in November, highlighting the importance of collaboration and early intervention to support those experiencing abuse and connect them with the resources they need. Through this partnership, called Safer Pathways, YWCA Calgary and FearIsNotLove staff will be embedded in DCU at the CPS headquarters, creating a more integrated approach to responding to family violence, supporting victims and addressing the complex needs of families in crisis. While the CPS DCU will continue to investigate the criminal aspects of family violence incidents, the co-location model will enable closer collaboration between police and community partners. By working together in the same space, the agencies will be able to share information more effectively, coordinate services and connect individuals with the supports they need at the earliest opportunity. "Family violence is a complex issue that often requires more than a criminal justice response," says Inspector Lee Wayne of the Calgary Police Service. "By bringing our partners together under one roof, we can better support victims, improve information sharing and connect families with the services they need sooner. This collaboration will help us create safer outcomes for those affected by family violence.” The partnership builds on the shared commitment of all three organizations to improve outcomes for those affected by family violence. By combining investigative expertise with specialized community supports, the co-location model will help ensure individuals and families receive timely, coordinated assistance that prioritizes both safety and long-term well-being. “YWCA Calgary is thrilled to begin a new partnership with Calgary Police Service and FearIsNotLove to offer faster community response and deeper long-term support to families in times of crisis” shares Talia Bell, CEO of YWCA Calgary. “Safer Pathways is an innovative new program that will provide a comprehensive approach to supporting all parties who are affected by domestic abuse.” “By working alongside the Calgary Police Service and YWCA Calgary, we can help ensure people impacted by family violence are connected to the right supports at the right time,” says Kim Ruse, CEO of FearIsNotLove. “A coordinated, compassionate response can make a meaningful difference in helping individuals and families find safety, access support and take steps toward a future free from abuse.” In addition to the Safer Pathways partnership, the CPS continues to partner with HomeFront to support survivors of family violence once charges are laid. Anyone experiencing abuse or violence in family or intimate relationships is encouraged to seek support in ways that feel safe for them. Free, confidential help is available by calling 211. Additional resources for those experiencing family violence are available through: The Domestic Violence and Abuse Helpline is available 24/7 at 403-234-SAFE (7233). FearIsNotLove co-ordinates the Men& program offering a variety of resources for men at 1-833-327-MENS (6367). The LUNA Child and Youth Advocacy Centre provides co-ordinated support for children and youth who have experienced abuse, as well as their families. Referrals to LUNA are made through partner agencies, including the CPS Child Abuse Unit. The Government of Alberta's Family Violence Info Line (310-1818), is available 24/7 in more than 170 languages anywhere in Alberta. If phone calls are not available, the Alberta Safety Chat Line is available between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m. ABT in English. Anyone experiencing family violence can contact the Calgary Police Service anytime by calling the non-emergency line at 403-266-1234, or 9-1-1 if in immediate danger.

title: Blackfoot Confederacy and City of Calgary building on progress under historic MOU
summary: T he Blackfoot Confederacy and The City of Calgary are building on progress made through their historic Memorandum of Understanding on Communication and Cooperation, building lasting relationships, strengthening collaboration and advancing shared priorities. Signed on May 9, 2025, the first-of-its-kind agreement for The City established a shared commitment to a stronger partnership between The Blackfoot Confederacy and The City of Calgary. It supports collaboration on shared priorities such as housing, arts and culture, economic development and tourism and events and communications, while creating a framework for regular dialogue, information-sharing and coordinated action. “A year and a half into this agreement, we have built meaningful relationships, deepened our understanding of one another and identified opportunities to move forward together,” said Mayor Jeromy Farkas. “There is still much work ahead, but our ongoing dialogue, mutual respect and shared commitment have reinforced the value of continuing this work as partners.” Turning shared priorities into action Since the MOU was signed, the partnership has strengthened and connected work already underway across shared priorities, including Indigenous housing, arts and culture. This includes improving how The City works with Indigenous housing applicants and advancing Indigenous-led housing, travelling exhibitions and public art initiatives. These early outcomes demonstrate how stronger relationships and shared understanding are helping turn shared priorities into action. “Mohkinstsis has always been an important place for Niitsitapi, and our relationship with this city carries both history and responsibility,” said Piikani Nation Chief and Blackfoot Confederacy President Troy Knowlton. “What we are building now is a stronger way to work together on the issues that affect our people today and future generations. This flag raising recognizes that relationship and the continued shared work that benefits our Blackfoot Nations and Calgarians.” Looking ahead Guided by the MOU, the Blackfoot Confederacy and The City will build on this progress by continuing to advance shared priorities in housing and houselessness, economic participation, arts and culture, and communications and engagement. The next phase will also focus on strengthening how this work is coordinated and guided to build capacity, remove barriers and create lasting benefits for Blackfoot Confederacy Nations and Calgarians. “Strong communities are built intentionally through relationships grounded in mutual benefit, accountability and respect,” said Katie Black, Acting Chief Operating Officer – City Services, The City of Calgary. “We share a responsibility to look beyond today and create opportunities for future generations to thrive. Our work to date has shown the importance of trust, listening and learning from one another — and while we, at The City, have deepened our understanding of Blackfoot history, perspectives and priorities, that learning is only beginning.” Through continued dialogue, shared accountability and action, the Blackfoot Confederacy and The City will build on this foundation and create lasting benefits for current and future generations. Learn more about the MOU and The City's work with Indigenous communities at calgary.ca .

title: Partners for Safety will help keep Calgary's little ghouls and goblins safe this Halloween
summary: Halloween is all about fun – not frights! For more than 30 years, Partners for Safety has helped Calgary kids trick-or-treat with confidence, and we're back again this year. On Saturday, Oct. 31, 2026, from 6 to 8 p.m., you'll see hundreds of vehicles out in the community, making sure families can enjoy a safe and happy Halloween night. The goals of the Partners for Safety program are to provide Halloween safety information to parents and children, and to patrol communities with a visible presence on Halloween night. Co-ordinated by Calgary's Child Magazine, the Partners for Safety include the Calgary Police Service (CPS), Emergency Health Services Alberta (EHS-Alberta), Calgary Fire Department (CFD), Calgary Transit, Calgary 9-1-1, and Peace Officers from Emergency Management and Community Safety. Any child experiencing a problem on Halloween can go to any one of these partners for help. During regular operations, the CPS and EHS-Alberta will have units patrolling residential neighbourhoods. The CFD will also have vehicles on patrol, and community fire stations will be open in between emergency responses as a safe place for trick-or-treaters to ask for help if they need it. Calgary Transit buses and CTrains are in the community day and night, providing essential transit services. On Halloween, if trick-or-treaters need help, they can approach any transit vehicle they spot. Bus and CTrain operators have radios and can contact the appropriate emergency personnel if needed. Important Health and Safety Tips: Keep pets contained and away from the front entrance; consider distributing treats outside. Use LED candles or lighting instead of real candles to create a spooky ambiance. Ensure sidewalks, front porches, and steps are well-lit and free of obstacles. Parents or guardians should inspect all candy before it is consumed. Halloween Tips for Kids: Inform your parent(s) or guardian(s) of your route, companions, and return time. Carry a cellphone in case plans change. Follow pedestrian rules: look both ways, walk instead of running, and cross streets at intersections. Complete trick-or-treating on one side of the street before crossing to the other. Wear bright, reflective clothing to enhance visibility to drivers. Avoid shortcuts through alleys, lanes, or private properties. Stay in well-lit, busy areas and carry a flashlight. Never enter a house or car while trick-or-treating. Trust your instincts; if something feels off, walk away and contact a parent or trusted adult, or approach a Partners for Safety vehicle. Before You Wear Your Costume: Test the full costume at home to ensure comfort and fit, making any necessary adjustments. Avoid very dark costumes; opt for bright colors and add reflective tape for visibility. Choose flame-resistant materials for costumes and accessories. Ensure costume accessories are soft, flexible, and free of sharp edges. Dress in layers to accommodate colder weather and ensure costumes are not too long to prevent tripping. Opt for comfortable masks or use make-up to avoid visibility issues. For more Halloween safety tips and fun ideas, visit calgaryschild.com or calgary.ca/halloweensafety .

title: Northeast Athletic Complex breaks ground on new opportunities for cricket, soccer and other sports in growing Calgary communities
summary: Construction is underway on the Northeast Athletic Complex (NEAC), adding much-needed indoor and outdoor recreation capacity in one of Calgary's fastest-growing areas. Located at 8500 40 St. N.E., the 35-acre, $170 million public recreation facility will serve people from northeast Calgary and across the city through Calgary's first competition-capable cricket field, four outdoor multi-use artificial turf fields and a 162,500 square foot indoor fieldhouse. It will include cricket batting nets, spectator areas and team spaces as well as pathways, green spaces, picnic areas and playgrounds to support gathering, active living and community use. “Breaking ground marks an important milestone in expanding recreation opportunities for people in Calgary,” shares Mayor Jeromy Farkas. “The Northeast Athletic Complex is an investment in more than fields and facilities. It's an investment in creating opportunities to be active, build connections and feel a sense of belonging.” “This is a turning point for cricket players and recreation users in Calgary and an important step toward meeting the growing needs of northeast communities,” said Ward 5 Councillor Raj Dhaliwal. “I am excited to see the opportunities this complex will create for people to play, compete and connect.” Public recreation facilities are essential community infrastructure. They give people places to be active, learn skills, connect with others and participate in community life. As Calgary grows, sustained investment is needed to renew aging facilities, add capacity and improve access in communities where recreation opportunities are limited. “Investing in recreation infrastructure helps meet Calgary's sport needs today and also sets us up to meet the needs of tomorrow,” said Ryan Atkinson, Acting Director of Public Spaces Delivery. “The Northeast Athletic Complex will add much-needed capacity in one of Calgary's fastest-growing areas and create more opportunities for sport, recreation and community connection.” The Northeast Athletic Complex advances GamePLAN, The City's 25-year vision and strategic framework for public recreation. Council adopted GamePLAN in 2025 and established Making Waves as the service level for public recreation facilities and amenities. Making Waves is the only funding scenario in which overall recreation service increases to match population growth, helping add capacity and improve access across Calgary. “Breaking ground on the Northeast Athletic Complex is an exciting moment. It marks an important step toward the addition of much-needed recreation and sport infrastructure in northeast Calgary," said Jarret Hoebers, Acting Director of Recreation & Social Programs. “This complex will add world-class amenities to our inventory and support the health and well-being of the community. This investment supports GamePLAN's long-term goal of more equitable access to recreation and sport opportunities across the city.” For more information and construction updates, please visit calgary.ca/NEAthleticComplex Quick facts The complex is located at 8500 40 Street N.E. The 35-acre site will include Calgary's first competition-capable cricket field, four outdoor multi-use artificial turf fields and a 162,500-square-foot indoor fieldhouse. The complex will also include cricket batting nets, soccer nets, spectator and team spaces, pathways, green spaces, picnic areas and playgrounds. Construction is anticipated to be completed in early 2029.

title: Five people charged in downtown drug trafficking investigation
summary: We have charged five people following an investigation into the sale of illicit drugs to members of vulnerable populations, in downtown Calgary. title: Calgary Conversations podcast: Honouring sacrifice on Remembrance Day
summary: CALGARY – As Calgarians prepare to honour our veterans, the Calgary Conversations podcast sits down with serving and former Armed Forces members to discuss the importance of Remembrance Day and the sacrifices made by those who serve and their families. Like so many Calgary businesses, the City of Calgary is proud to employ veterans and reservists. For this episode, we sit down with three City staff members to discuss their connection to the Canadian military and how the lessons learned in service of our country have translated into municipal public service. Iain Bushell, Director of Emergency Management and Community Safety and a former member of the Royal Canadian Air Force for more than a decade, recounts the foundational leadership skills he learned in the Air Force and how it serves him in his role today. Mitch Walz, Associate Assessor at the City and an Infantry Officer the Calgary Highlanders Reserve Regiment, speaks about the often-forgotten sacrifices made by families of reservists and military members. Vladimir Batinic, a Team Lead with Technical Security, speaks about the importance of remembering those that came before and those who are currently making commitments to our nation. The three sit down for an emotional and honest look at the camaraderie of service and the importance of remembering those who served and came home, those who served and came home different, and those who didn't come back home at all. Listen to their stories at calgary.ca or wherever you download your favourite podcasts. Check out past episodes at Calgary Conversations: The City of Calgary podcast . -30-

title: Calgary Fire Responds to House Fire in Garrison Green
summary: At around 2:00pm fire crews responded the 0-100 block of Mike Ralph Way SW for a structure fire. Crews arrived at a two-story residential home with a front attached garage with large flames coming from the garage area. There were two vehicles on the driveway on fire as flames were also rapidly spreading up the front exterior of the home and into the second floor. Firefighters quickly stretched hose lines and began knocking back the fire as other firefighters made entry to the home for an interior fire attack and search for occupants. Crews reported encountering zero visibility and heavy smoke conditions throughout the second floor. The fire had spread to the attic space and roof area. There were no occupants found inside and no injuries were reported. A ladder truck water tower was set up as fire crews shifted tactics to apply large volume water from the exterior. Once the fire was sufficiently knocked down, firefighters re-entered the home to extinguish remaining hot spots. The source home sustained heavy damage, and the occupants will be displaced. The two neighbouring homes are being assessed for heat damage. Calgary Police Services, Emergency Health Services Alberta, ATCO Gas and Enmax all attended the scene. A fire investigator is on scene and has begun their investigation into the origin and cause of the fire. A fire watch crew is also on scene to monitor conditions. -30-

title: Bearspaw South Feeder Main reaches 95% installation; construction to connect the new feeder main and Stage 4 water restrictions begin November 4
summary: Construction on the Bearspaw South Feeder Main Replacement Project is nearing completion, with approximately 95 per cent of the new feeder main now installed across stages A and B. The project is entering its final stages, with work beginning in November to connect the new feeder main to the existing water system. "We are not out of the woods yet, but we are getting very close," states Michael Thompson, Chief Operating Officer for the Water Utility. “On November 4 we will start work to connect the new pipe to our water system, keeping us on track to have the new pipe in service by the end of the year.” In order to safely complete the connection, the existing feeder main will need to be shut down for approximately four weeks. Stage 4 outdoor water restrictions will be in place, and indoor water conservation is needed starting November 4. Stage A construction update Stage A construction began in January and used microtunnelling to complete approximately 3.7 kilometres of tunnelling. Installation of both the concrete carrier pipe and the new steel feeder main between the Shaganappi Pump Station and 73 Street N.W. was completed in September. Stage A construction continues and crews have now completed grouting in the space between the carrier pipe and the new steel feeder main. Construction in the valve chambers and work on supporting infrastructure are ongoing. Stage B construction update Stage B open-cut construction along 34 Avenue N.W. in Bowness began in June and remains on schedule. More than 90 per cent of the new feeder main has now been installed between 89 Street N.W. and 73 Street N.W. As pipe installation progresses, crews are restoring roadways, sidewalks and property access along the alignment. Landscaping restoration will continue through the fall, weather permitting. Any remaining work will be completed in spring 2027. Connecting the feeder main Starting November 4, crews will begin preparing to connect, or “tie-in”, the pipe by shutting down and draining the existing Bearspaw South Feeder Main. Tie-in construction will take place in November and December at three locations: 33 and 34 Avenues N.W. and 83 Street N.W. 33 Avenue N.W. and 89 Street N.W. Shaganappi Pump Station, near Edworthy Park This work will result in significant traffic impacts, including intersection and lane closures, detours, and sidewalk and bicycle lane closures. Construction hours will vary by location, with some work requiring 24-hour construction. Stage 4 water restrictions Connecting the new feeder main to the existing water system will take approximately four weeks. During this time, the existing Bearspaw South Feeder Main will be temporarily shut down, significantly reducing how much water can be distributed across the city. As a result, city-wide Stage 4 outdoor water restrictions and voluntary indoor water conservation will be required beginning November 4 for approximately four weeks. While the feeder main is shut down, every water-saving action will help reduce demand on Calgary's water system. We're asking Calgarians to prepare to conserve water by not watering outdoors, flushing only when needed, running dishwashers and washing machines with full loads and taking shorter showers (aiming for three minutes or less). We're also encouraging everyone to help spread the word that water restrictions begin November 4 by sharing this information with family and friends. Parkdale Boulevard repairs Starting October 29, additional repairs will be completed on a different section of the feeder main between the Shaganappi Pump Station and the Memorial Pump Station along Parkdale Boulevard N.W. Assessments of this pipe show it remains in good overall condition but requires proactive repairs in six locations. The repairs will require work at six locations at the same time, with a dedicated crew at each site. We will excavate and replace sections of the existing pipe with new steel segments. Lane closures and traffic detours will be in place along Parkdale Boulevard N.W., and river pathway detours will be required in the area. Be prepared for traffic delays on Parkdale Boulevard and consider planning an alternate route for your commute. Work on Parkdale Boulevard is expected to be completed in early December. Community support The City continues to work directly with residents, businesses and property owners affected by construction. Residents experiencing construction-related impacts can visit the Bearspaw South Feeder Main Community Resource Centre at the Bowness Community Association, 7904 43 Ave. N.W. The Centre is open: Monday and Wednesday: 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tuesday and Thursday: 10 a.m. to 7 p.m. Bearspaw South Feeder Main Construction Liaisons are also available at the Community Resource Centre on Wednesdays from 10 a.m. to noon. For project information and construction updates, visit calgary.ca/bearspawfeedermain .

title: Police use intelligence to target drug trafficking through Operation Guardian

Officers within OCEU use this analysis to deploy to these areas to disrupt criminal activity, collect intelligence and conduct investigations and enforcement. title: Calgary volunteers plant more than 8,500 trees to help grow our urban forest
summary: More than 1,200 volunteers supported The City's Urban Forestry team this spring and summer to plant 8,570 trees, helping create a greener, healthier Calgary for generations to come. From June through September, community associations, local businesses, organizations and individual Calgarians dug in to help grow Calgary's urban forest through The City's Volunteer Tree Planting Program. Together, volunteers took part in 35 planting events at 21 locations across 19 communities, with 28 different volunteer groups contributing to this year's success. In total, 8,570 trees were planted, including 1,500 whips (small saplings), which, as they grow, will create a greener city that will benefit Calgarians for decades to come. “We are incredibly grateful to the volunteers and partner groups who contributed their time and energy to help grow Calgary's urban forest," said Randi Kelley, Urban Forestry Field Coordinator, City of Calgary, Parks and Open Spaces. "Their enthusiasm and commitment have made a difference in our communities. The trees they planted will provide shade, beauty and environmental benefits for generations of Calgarians to come. We couldn't do this work without them.” One of this year's planting highlights took place at Ted Harrison School in Taradale, where volunteers planted over 2,000 trees over five planting events. The trees were planted in multiple beds arranged in creative configurations, transforming an area of the school grounds into what students are already calling their very own “maze." While the trees are still young, students are excited to watch their mini forest grow and change over the coming years. As the trees mature, they'll help create a greener, more inviting schoolyard, providing shade, opportunities to connect with nature and lasting benefits for students, families and the surrounding community. The success of the Volunteer Tree Planting Program is made possible through partnerships with community groups, local businesses and organizations, including Trees for Life, one of The City's planting partners. "We at Trees for Life applaud the City of Calgary's efforts to double their urban tree canopy," said Mike Hurley, Development Director, Trees for Life. “We are proud to offer any support we can to help advance the progress toward this ambitious goal and to help engage the local community in the process. Trees are not only vital to the overall health of a vibrant urban community, but they are a phenomenal way to thank and engage local groups and individuals who also contribute to the overall wellbeing of the community.” These community planting efforts also support The City's long-term goal of increasing Calgary's urban tree canopy coverage to 16 per cent by 2060. Calgary's most recent tree canopy measurement was 9.62 per cent in 2024, and every new tree planted helps move us toward that target as it grows and matures. Anyone interested in helping grow Calgary's urban forest can visit calgary.ca/volunteertreeplanting ⁠ to learn more about the Volunteer Tree Planting Program and check back in spring 2027 for next season's planting opportunities. For more information on caring for Calgary's trees, please visit calgary.ca/trees .

title: City of Calgary reminds residents: Celebrate Diwali and Bandi Chhor Divas safely
summary: As Diwali and Bandi Chhor Divas approach, The City of Calgary, Calgary Fire Department (CFD), Emergency Management & Community Safety (EMCS) and Calgary Police Service (CPS) are wishing everyone a happy, safe and joyful festival season. These celebrations hold deep cultural significance for many Calgarians and are celebrated in homes, places of worship and communities across our city. As families and communities prepare to celebrate, it's important to understand Calgary's rules around fireworks and how to celebrate safely. Personal fireworks are not permitted in Calgary. This includes fireworks purchased outside Calgary or ordered online. Fireworks can quickly cause fires, injuries and property damage. "Happy Diwali and Bandi Chhor Divas to everyone celebrating across Calgary," says Glenn Baxter, Fire Marshal with CFD. "Fireworks can quickly ignite grass, vehicles and homes. We've seen first-hand how one firework can lead to significant property damage and put lives at risk. We ask residents to celebrate responsibly and be mindful of those around them." During Diwali 2025, CPS received 167 fireworks-related calls, and The City received 44, 311 reports. CFD crews responded to several fires caused by fireworks, including grass fires, a vehicle fire and a structure fire. In one incident, hundreds of individuals discharged thousands of fireworks over several hours, requiring a significant police response. Updated fines now in effect To improve public safety, The City recently strengthened fireworks enforcement. Effective Sept. 22, 2026, fines increased and a new offence was introduced for carrying or setting up fireworks in public places before they are discharged. Current penalties include: Selling or offering fireworks for sale without authorization: $3,000 Possessing fireworks in a public place: $1,000 Discharging fireworks without a permit: $1,000 "These changes close an important gap in our enforcement tools," says Damian Cole, Deputy Chief of Community Safety. "Officers can now intervene when fireworks are being prepared for use in public spaces, helping prevent dangerous situations before they occur." "We want everyone to enjoy these celebrations safely and respectfully," says Geoff Gawlinski, Staff Sergeant with CPS. "Last year, officers responded to numerous fireworks-related complaints, including reports that were initially believed to be gunshots. Unauthorized fireworks can create safety concerns and place significant demands on emergency services.” Illegal fireworks sales remain prohibited The City is also reminding businesses that selling fireworks without a permit is illegal in Calgary. "Selling fireworks without authorization is against the law and carries significant penalties,” says Michael Briegel, Deputy Chief of Business Safety. “Businesses must understand the regulations and ensure they are operating in compliance with Calgary's bylaws.” Celebrate safely The City recognizes that fireworks are an important part of Diwali celebrations for many people and there is no perfect substitute. However, Calgary's restrictions are in place to protect families, neighbours and communities. Residents are encouraged to light diyas safely, use LED candles, decorate with festive lights, attend community celebrations, and gather with family and friends. Small birthday cake sparklers are exempt from the bylaw, but must be used safely and responsibly. "Safety is a shared responsibility," says Glenn Baxter. "By understanding the rules and making informed choices, we can help ensure everyone enjoys a safe and memorable celebration." Please report illegal fireworks concerns to 311, using the category “Disturbance and Public Behaviour Concerns” and including details about the location. Call 9-1-1 to report a fire or emergency. For more information, visit www.calgary.ca/fireworks . For information on safer Diwali practices, visit www.calgary.ca/Diwali .

title: Man charged in bank investigator fraud scam that impersonated police and financial institutions
summary: The Calgary Police Service Financial Crime Investigation Unit's Fraud Team has charged one man in relation to a bank investigator fraud scam in which offenders allegedly impersonated financial institutions and Calgary police officers using caller ID spoofing technology. Between Saturday, June 7, 2025, and Monday, July 14, 2025, the Calgary Police Service received several reports of bank investigator fraud scams. In these scams, offenders use caller ID spoofing technology to display legitimate financial institution customer service telephone numbers on victims' caller ID. The calls appear to originate from the victims' financial institution. Offenders then falsely claim unauthorized transactions have compromised the victims' accounts and linked them to criminal activity. Victims are then directed to speak with individuals posing as Calgary police officers and instructed to place their bank cards in envelopes for courier pickup from their homes. The cards and associated banking information are then used to conduct unauthorized ATM withdrawals and point-of-sale purchases. Through CCTV footage, investigators identified a suspect allegedly purchasing and redeeming gift cards. The suspect was arrested on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. As a result, Imani Lionel CROSS, 26, of Calgary, is charged with one count of fraud over $5,000, two counts of possession of property obtained by crime and one count of laundering the proceeds of crime. CROSS was also arrested on an outstanding warrant. CROSS is scheduled to appear in court on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. By the numbers: Bank and police impersonation scams continue to be an emerging trend across Canada and are not isolated to Calgary or the Calgary Police Service. We have also seen offenders pose as RCMP officers and direct victims to transfer cryptocurrency or deposit money into Bitcoin ATMs. Police services across the country continue to investigate these scams and work to identify and hold those responsible accountable. In 2025, we received 24 reports involving both bank and police impersonation, compared with seven reports so far in 2026. For police impersonation scams specifically, we received 171 reports in 2025, compared with 27 reports so far in 2026. The 2026 statistics are current as of Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026. We continue to encourage Calgarians to remain vigilant when contacted by anyone claiming to represent a financial institution, police service or another trusted organization. Police will never ask you to send money, transfer cryptocurrency or deposit funds into a Bitcoin ATM as part of an investigation. Fraud prevention tips: The Calgary Police Service reminds citizens that: · Financial institutions and police will never ask you to mail bank cards, provide banking credentials, send money or make purchases as part of an investigation. · Be cautious of unexpected calls, emails or text messages claiming to be from your bank, police or another trusted organization. Fraudsters can spoof phone numbers and create convincing messages that appear legitimate. · When in doubt, delete suspicious messages or hang up, then contact the organization directly using an official phone number or website to verify the request. · Never share personal information, banking information, passwords or verification codes with an unsolicited caller or sender. · If you feel pressured to act immediately or something does not seem right, stop the conversation and speak with a trusted friend, family member or co-worker before taking any action. title: Boil Water Advisory has been rescinded for Eagle Ridge
summary: CALGARY – Effective immediately, Alberta Health Services has rescinded the Boil Water Advisory for the community of Eagle Ridge. The Boil Water Advisory remains for Heritage Park. Heritage Park is a working directly with Alberta Health Services to ensure testing requirement are met for their site. The City of Calgary labs, in collaboration with Alberta Health Services (AHS) and Alberta Environment and Protected Areas) have tested and confirmed that the water in Eagle Ridge meet water-quality guidelines and standards and is safe for consuming. If you have used your household or business water in the past 24 hours, it can now be safely consumed without boiling. If you have not used your household or business water in the past 24 hours, you should flush your system. To flush your household or business water system: ➡️ Turn the bathtub tap on cold for ten minutes. Then turn all other faucets on cold for five minutes. ➡️ For businesses without a bathtub or shower, turn on all your faucets on cold for ten minutes. The City of Calgary thanks affected residents and businesses for their patience and cooperation during this time. For more information visit calgary.ca/boilwater or contact 311.

title: City awards two sites to affordable housing providers under non-market land sale program
summary: Calgary, AB — The City of Calgary has awarded two sites approved for disposition under the fifth Non-Market Housing Land Sale (NMLS) Program to affordable housing providers Liberty Housing Organization and Siksika Off-Reserve Affordable Housing (SORAH). The awarded sites are: 155 Cirrus Cl N.E.: Liberty Housing Organization with an envisioned 105 homes for Calgarians 3010 36 St S.E.: SORAH with an envisioned 95 homes for Indigenous Calgarians The NMLS program uses surplus City-owned land to reduce project costs, provide equity and help non-profit providers secure financing and government funding. Each dollar of City land value has leveraged nearly $4.50 from provincial and federal partners. $3.9 million in the form of a land value contribution is being invested in these two projects in total. Also included in NMLS round five was a site located at 15 Santana HL NW, however the applications received did not meet program requirements. The City will not proceed with the awarding of this site in this phase and it will be offered in a future NMLS round. "The need for affordable housing in our city is greater than ever,” says Mayor Jeromy Farkas. “Offering City-owned land to select providers at below market value helps to remove land cost, which is one of the largest barriers facing non-profit housing providers, and helps us to provide more homes for Calgarians.” Both housing providers must now carry out further due diligence to ensure the sites are viable for their projects, and must satisfy their pre-sale conditions, including land use amendments where applicable and development permit approvals. "We are honoured to have been selected through the City's Non-Market Land Sale to transform the Midfield Heights site at 155 Cirrus Close NE into high-quality, non-market housing.” says President of Liberty Housing Organization Oliver Trutina. “This opportunity marks an important step toward expanding affordable housing options and providing more Calgarians with safe, stable homes. We look forward to continuing our partnership with the City of Calgary to help close the housing affordability gap and build more inclusive communities." "The team at SORAH Project is thrilled to continue working with the City of Calgary to create sustainable, vibrant and culturally significant housing solutions for urban Indigenous peoples in the City,” says SORAH General Manager Max Lloyd. “The Dover project will see the construction of close to 100 townhomes, which is critical to helping address the need for affordable housing in Calgary.” Since 2019, NMLS has enabled nearly 1,000 perpetually affordable homes across 18 developments; 280 homes have opened their doors to date with more than 700 in active planning or construction. Learn more about the initiative and find housing resources at calgary.ca/affordablehousing .

title: Western Inland Ports form alliance to strengthen Canada's trade corridors
summary: CentrePort Canada, Global Transportation Hub Authority, Leduc County, Edmonton Global and Edmonton Airports (Port Alberta), and The City of Calgary and Rocky View County (Prairie Economic Gateway) have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to create the Canadian Inland Ports Alliance (CIPA). The Alliance will align on major inland port initiatives, strengthening seaport-to-hinterland connectivity and supporting a more resilient, diversified, and competitive Canadian trade network. CIPA responds directly to growing pressures facing Canada's trade and transportation network, including congestion, shifting trade partners, supply chain disruptions, marine gateway constraints and the need for stronger inland capacity. The Alliance will help speed up coordinated action, increase interprovincial trade, expand access to global markets, and strengthen supply chain reliability. The MoU establishes a framework for formal collaboration on planning, advocacy, investment, and performance measurement. The agreement is intended to advance strategic planning focused on Canadian inland ports, aligning priorities, and advancing shared evidence to measure progress and outcomes. The parties will review progress annually and identify opportunities for further collaboration. Quotes “Inland ports play a vital role in strengthening Canada's trade and transportation networks. The Government of Canada is committed to expanding trade opportunities and building resilient supply chains. By investing in modern transportation infrastructure across the country, we are helping ensure the efficient movement of goods while supporting local jobs and economic growth.” - The Honourable Steven MacKinnon, Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons “Prairie Economic Gateway was created to help address Canada's trade challenges by increasing capacity in the trade network and creating new routes to more markets. This agreement shows how municipalities, inland ports and regions can work together to strengthen trade infrastructure, make supply chains more reliable and support a stronger Canadian economy.” - Mayor Jeromy Farkas, City of Calgary “Prairie Economic Gateway is a generational opportunity to strengthen our region's role in Canadian trade, attract investment and create long-term economic opportunity. By coordinating our efforts and planning across the trade corridor, we can help Western Canadian businesses move goods more efficiently and support a more resilient, diversified economy.” - Reeve Sunny Samra, Rocky View County “Canada's trade volumes are growing, and strong, integrated national trade corridors are integral to our sovereignty and connectivity. Inland ports build capacity and resiliency into our national transportation network. As Canada's largest and most established inland port, we have seen firsthand the value inland ports provide for Canadian businesses: More options to move their goods to market, room to invest and grow, and the ability to more easily build resilient and diversified supply chains.” - Carly Edmundson, President & CEO, CentrePort Canada Inc. “Port Alberta is a critical link in Canada's trade network, and the Canadian Inland Ports Alliance will unlock new value across it. By connecting Western Canada's inland ports more directly to global markets, we're opening new routes to market and real revenue opportunities for Canadian and international businesses ready to grow.” – Daryn Edgar, CEO Edmonton Global “As an airport CEO, I recognize that Canada's aviation network is part of a national, multimodal transport system. This MOU reflects our joint efforts to invest in data, deepen our understanding of trade flows, and modernize digital trade strategies—unlocking more efficient intermodal transport and delivering greater value for Canadians.” - Myron Keehn, President and CEO, Edmonton Airports “Trade has always been a cornerstone of Saskatchewan's economy. The Canadian Inland Ports Alliance unites key transportation and logistics partners to strengthen Canada's trade infrastructure, improve access to global markets and build a more connected and resilient supply chain network. Together, we are helping position Canada and Saskatchewan for long-term economic growth and competitiveness.” - Daniel Hersche, President and CEO, The Global Transportation Hub Authority “Leduc County proudly supports the Canadian Inland Ports Alliance, an initiative highlighting the importance of provincial and regional partnerships in driving economic growth across Alberta and Canada. Our County is uniquely positioned to help make this initiative a success by leveraging key assets. These include the Edmonton International Airport (YEG) with its 24/7 global cargo hub, the Nisku Business Park, home to more than 800 businesses and 15,000 employees, and our strategic access to major rail and road networks that move goods and services quickly and efficiently.” – Mayor Tanni Doblanko, Leduc County -30- About CentrePort Canada CentrePort Canada is a 20,000-acre inland port and Foreign Trade Zone. Located in the heart of North America, CentrePort connects to major national and international trade gateways and corridors, and is the only inland port in the country with direct access to tri-modal transportation – extensive truck, rail and air cargo operations. www.centreportcanada.ca About the Global Transportation Hub Authority The Global Transportation Hub Authority (GTH) is Saskatchewan's inland port and one of Canada's premier inland logistics hubs. Located in Regina, Saskatchewan, the GTH provides strategic access to rail, highway, and supply chain infrastructure that connects businesses to markets across North America and around the world. The GTH supports investment attraction, industrial development, and the efficient movement of goods, strengthening Saskatchewan's role in Canada's trade network. About Port Alberta Port Alberta helps businesses unlock new value from the Edmonton Metropolitan Region. In North America's northernmost major inland port. Here, air, rail, pipelines and highways converge, giving Canadian and international companies a direct path to new markets, new customers and new revenue. For businesses ready to grow, a world of opportunity starts here. About Prairie Economic Gateway Prairie Economic Gateway is a regionally approved, shovel-ready collaboration between The City of Calgary and Rocky View County to enable rail-served industrial development and economic diversification in the Calgary region. Gateway is envisioned as the centre of a future inland port supported by private sector investment. By extending trade infrastructure capacity beyond Canada's congested seaports and into the Prairies, the project is intended to strengthen national supply chains, open new opportunities for industrial development, and support long-term economic growth in Alberta and across Canada. title: Calgarians invited to help shape future of arts and culture
summary: As Calgary continues to grow and change, The City is inviting residents to help shape an updated cultural plan for Calgary through public engagement until Nov. 15. The cultural plan will help guide the future of arts, culture, music and Calgary's creative economy. More than a plan for funding, it will establish a long-term cultural vision to guide future investments, policy, partnerships and strategies as the city evolves. Input from Calgarians, partners, artists, organizations and communities will help inform the plan's direction. Arts and culture contribute to community wellbeing, vibrant neighbourhoods and communities, tourism, talent attraction and economic growth. An updated cultural plan will help ensure Calgary continues to benefit from those contributions while identifying opportunities to improve access to arts and culture across the city. "Arts and culture are part of how we experience Calgary every day," says Franca Gualtieri, manager of Arts & Culture at The City of Calgary. "Whether it's a festival, gathering place, cultural tradition or creative experience, these things help shape our city and connect us to one another. We're encouraging Calgarians to share what matters to them to help inform the updated cultural plan." The first Cultural Plan for Calgary was published in 2016 and helped provide a shared vision for arts and culture over the past decade. This project is an opportunity to build on that foundation and develop a cultural plan that supports Calgary for the next 30 years. Calgarians can participate by taking the online survey, joining an online information session or attending an open house. Details about all engagement opportunities are available at calgary.ca/culturalplan . Feedback gathered through this phase of engagement will be summarized in a What We Heard Report and used to help shape the next phase of public and sector engagement in spring 2027. The proposed cultural plan will be presented to Council in late 2027.

title: Man charged after breaching court-ordered release conditions in 48 hours

On Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, YOUNGMAN was released with court-ordered conditions involving a 24-hour curfew and a weapons prohibition.
