title: Confined Space Rescue in the NW
summary: At approximately 8:40 a.m., Calgary Fire Department crews responded to a confined space rescue at a construction site in the 8000 block of 34 Avenue N.W. Upon arrival, firefighters located a construction worker who had fallen approximately 30 feet down a manhole at the site. Crews safely accessed the patient using air-monitoring equipment and initiated patient care, stabilizing the individual while preparing for removal. The Calgary Fire Department's Technical Rescue Team was dispatched and established a rope rescue system to safely extricate the worker from the confined space. Once stabilized and packaged for transport, the patient was successfully removed from the manhole using the rope rescue system. The patient's care was then transferred to Alberta Health Services, and the individual was transported to hospital in stable condition. Calgary Police Service also attended the scene to assist. As this incident involved a workplace injury, Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) was notified and was enroute to investigate. The Calgary Fire Department would like to recognize the coordinated efforts of all responding agencies whose collaboration contributed to the successful rescue. -30-

title: Joint operation results in 19 arrests and 87 warrants executed
summary: A joint warrant enforcement operation between the Calgary Police Service and Alberta Sheriffs has resulted in 19 arrests and the execution of 87 outstanding warrants. The recent two-day operation brought together members of our District 3 Community Engagement Response Team (CERT), Community Resource Officers (CRO), Patrol Officers and the Fugitive Apprehension Sheriff Support Team (FASST). The initiative focused on locating wanted fugitives, improving public safety and furthering investigations. The operation was planned over several weeks, with analytical resources preparing and reviewing approximately 130 information packages before officers were deployed. During the operation, members attended 62 residences throughout District 3. The operation resulted in: 19 individuals arrested. 87 warrants executed for charges including possession of dangerous weapons, drug trafficking, personation, possession of stolen property and possession of fake ID documents. “Our continuing partnership with the Alberta Sheriffs allows us to improve community safety, by coordinating resources to hold offenders accountable, while addressing ongoing concerns within the district,” says District 3 Insp. Travis Juska. “Strong collaboration between law enforcement agencies is essential to keeping Alberta communities safe. Operations like this demonstrate what we can accomplish when the Alberta Sheriffs and our policing partners work together, share resources and use our combined expertise to locate wanted fugitives and hold offenders accountable,” says Insp. Darren Thompson with the Alberta Sheriffs FASST. The Calgary Police Service extends its thanks to the Alberta Sheriffs for their continued collaboration and support.

title: Council appoints remaining members to Calgary's Water Utility Oversight Board
summary: Council's appointment of four members to Calgary's Water Utility Oversight Board (The Board) marks an important milestone in strengthening independent oversight of Calgary's water utility. Kate Chisholm, Corey Goulet, Edward McCauley and Kim Sturgess will join Stephen Stanley, who was named the inaugural Chair last month. These appointments complete the five-member board being established in response to recommendations from the Bearspaw South Feedermain Independent Review Panel. “We were looking for people who would bring different perspectives to the table, work effectively together and understand the important governance role of the WUOB,” said Steve Stanley, Board Chair. “Together, we have the breadth of experience needed to provide thoughtful, independent advice while keeping a clear focus on the long-term reliability and sustainability of Calgary's water utility.” The members were selected through a skills-based recruitment process supported by an external recruitment firm. It focused on finding individuals with experience in governance, regulatory environments, engineering, critical utility operations, finance, risk management, environmental science and executive utility leadership. “Independent oversight is an important part of a strong and accountable water utility,” said Michael Thompson, COO - Water Utility. “We welcome the perspective The Board will bring alongside Administration's operational knowledge and expertise. I look forward to working together to strengthen decision-making and support a water system Calgarians can rely on for generations to come.” The new members are: Kate Chisholm is an experienced corporate director with C-suite experience spanning legal and regulatory matters, risk management, environmental policy, sustainability and communications. A lawyer by training, she has held senior leadership roles with organizations including Capital Power Corporation, EPCOR Utilities and the Alberta Electric System Operator, and brings extensive board experience. Corey Goulet is a senior energy infrastructure executive with extensive experience in major capital projects, engineering and operations. A mechanical engineer by training, he has held senior leadership roles with Trans Mountain, TC Energy, Kiewit, Steelhead LNG and Tundra Energy Marketing, and brings significant experience working in regulated environments. Edward McCauley is an experienced leader and environmental scientist with extensive governance, research and organizational leadership experience. He has served as President and Vice-Chancellor of the University of Calgary since 2019 and has held leadership roles in water and environmental research, including with the Alberta Ingenuity Centre for Water Research and Alberta Water Research Institute. Kim Sturgess is an engineer and business leader with deep expertise in water management, governance and policy. She is the founder and former CEO of WaterSMART Solutions, where she spent more than two decades helping industrial, municipal and government clients improve the management of Alberta's water resources. She also brings extensive governance experience, including roles with the Alberta Water Council, Alberta Chamber of Resources board, Calgary Airport Authority and National Research Council of Canada. With the appointments now complete, board members will participate in onboarding and orientation before beginning their formal work. The first board meeting is planned for later this year.

title: Trust in The City reaches highest level since 2018 as resident confidence grows
summary: CALGARY – The City's 2026 Fall Research Results are now available to the public, prior to the presentation to City Council on October 27, 2026. The results suggest Calgarians are becoming more positive about life in Calgary and more confident in municipal government, while continuing to hold high expectations for infrastructure, safety and future growth. Quality of life, satisfaction with City services, trust in The City and perceptions of value for tax dollars all increased compared with fall 2025. “One of the clearest findings in this year's research is growing confidence in Calgary's future and in The City of Calgary as its municipal government,” says Chief Administrative Officer David Duckworth. “ That confidence is also reflected nationally, with Calgary outperforming comparable Canadian municipalities on key measures including quality of life, service satisfaction, trust and value for tax dollars. But greater confidence also comes with high expectations. Our responsibility is to turn that optimism into action and keep delivering for Calgarians as our city grows.” Confidence in Calgary is improving This year's research shows improvement across several key indicators that reflect how Calgarians feel about Calgary and municipal government. · 77 per cent rate their quality of life as good, up from 71 per cent last year. · 73 per cent are satisfied with City services, up from 67 per cent in fall 2025. · 49 per cent say they receive good value for their municipal tax dollars, up from 42 per cent in fall 2025. · 56 per cent trust The City, up from 47 per cent last year and the highest level recorded since 2018. Trust and service satisfaction continue to rise Trust and satisfaction showed some of the strongest gains in this year's research. Since last fall, trust in The City increased by nine per cent (47 per cent), while dissatisfaction declined from 24 per cent to 16 per cent. Service satisfaction also improved significantly, reaching its highest level since 2019. The findings suggest that trust grows when residents feel The City is running Calgary well, responding to community needs and working collaboratively. Perceptions of value for tax dollars are strongest when residents are satisfied with City services and believe public funds are being spent responsibly. Calgarians continue to prioritize transportation, infrastructure and safety While residents are expressing growing confidence in Calgary and municipal government, they continue to identify several issues they want The City to prioritize. · Traffic and roads remain the most frequently identified priority at 36 per cent. · Crime, safety and policing ranks second at 23 per cent. · Homelessness, poverty and affordable housing follows at 18 per cent. · Transit remains among the top priorities at 15 per cent. The research also found increased mentions of pedestrian safety, water infrastructure and aggressive driving compared with previous surveys. This year's findings suggest confidence is growing, while Calgarians remain focused on the issues that matter to them. The results suggest strong support for infrastructure investment, with 82 per cent of Calgarians agreeing now is a good time for The City to invest in new projects like roads, public transportation and local facilities. Residents recognize progress while continuing to expect visible improvements in the services and infrastructure that support Calgary's future. Calgary outperforms other major Canadian cities National Municipal Benchmarking results show Calgary scores above comparable municipalities on several key measures. Compared with national benchmarks, Calgary scores: · 8 per cent higher on quality of life · 7 per cent higher on service satisfaction · 12 per cent higher on trust · 6 per cent higher on value for tax dollars These results provide important context as many of the pressures affecting Calgarians, including affordability, growth and economic uncertainty, are also affecting municipalities across Canada. Research helps measure Calgarians' priorities and perceptions The results of this representative, third-party survey, together with additional research, provide City Council with insights into Calgarians' views on a range of issues, including quality of life, City services and Calgary's future. As one of the only cities in Canada to conduct biannual surveys on government performance and public sentiment, The City's public research results also help provide ongoing accountability and transparency to Calgarians, while identifying strengths and opportunities for improvement. The 2026 Fall Survey of Calgarians was conducted by Ipsos Public Affairs from August 4, 2026 to August 28, 2026 with 2,500 Calgarians, via telephone. The survey was conducted using numbers from both cell phones (70 per cent) and landlines (30 per cent) to obtain a random and statistically representative sample of Calgarians with a margin of error ± 2.0 percentage points, 19 times out of 20. The 2026 Fall Survey of Calgarians report as well as other research can be found at calgary.ca/insights . The fall survey presentation will be available on October 27. -30-

title: Safety in the classroom: Calgary Fire appeals to educators, parents and students for their continued partnership in annual School Fire Drill Program
summary: Calgary firefighters visit hundreds of schools across the city annually to perform school fire drills. All schools in Calgary must complete six fire drills per school year, and one of these drills should be attended by the Calgary Fire Department (CFD). Through this program, firefighters and school staff can practice and access their evacuation procedures, reinforce life safety messages with students and families and connect teachers with fire safety educational resources. The drills also reinforce the importance of planning and rehearsing an escape plan not only at school, but at the children's homes. CFD's appeal for fire safety awareness comes at a time where residential fires are on the rise. Although overall fire-related incidents were comparable to last year's levels, Calgary's single-family residential fires were up over 28% in September 2026 compared to 2025. On October 22, members of CFD, along with representatives from the Calgary Catholic School District, conducted a school fire drill at St. Elizabeth Seton School. Fire Chief Steve Dongworth, along with newly-appointed Junior Fire Chief Kean Hallisey, activated the fire alarm in the school, ensuring that it works, while evacuating children and staff safely. They also emphasized the importance of having a home escape plan in the event of an emergency. Greg Moore, Senior Officer, Occupational Health & Safety, Calgary Catholic School District said “by teaching our students about fire prevention and the importance of making safe choices, we're helping them build habits that can protect themselves, their families, their schools and their communities. We're grateful to the Calgary Fire Department for helping bring these lessons to life for our students”. “CFD is actively working with all the schools in Calgary to teach children about the importance of fire safety and practicing escape plans at home with their families” said Fire Chief Steve Dongworth. “We're helping students to build habits that protect themselves, their families and their schools.” To learn more about school fire drills, visit calgary.ca/schoolfiredrills -30-

title: Construction begins on Walden Fire Station and Library
summary: Residents in Calgary's growing southeast will gain a permanent fire station and a new public library in one shared community hub, with construction now underway on the Walden Fire Station and Library. With an estimated project cost of $34.2 million, the project will create Calgary's first integrated fire station and public library. The facility, located at 969 Walden Drive S.E., will include a permanent two-bay fire station and a new Calgary Public Library location serving residents of Walden, Legacy, Chaparral, Wolf Willow and surrounding communities. The facility is anticipated to open in 2028. “This project reflects the kind of thoughtful infrastructure investment that helps build a more connected, resilient and livable Calgary,” says Mayor Jeromy Farkas. “By bringing essential services together in one location and making efficient use of public resources, we're creating lasting value for residents and helping build thriving communities.” The Government of Alberta contributed $4.1 million toward the project through the Local Government Fiscal Framework and the former Municipal Sustainability Initiative, supporting the delivery of this investment in Calgary's southeast. "The Walden Fire Station and Library is a prime example of creative thinking about municipal infrastructure,” says Dan Williams, Alberta Minister of Municipal Affairs. “ Through Municipal Affairs ' more than $4 million investment, our government is proud to help create family-focused spaces that will improve livability and inspire Calgary citizens long into the future." "This project represents the first public civic infrastructure built in Ward 14 since 1976,” says Landon Johnston, Councillor for Ward 14. "It represents the start of what we hope to be many, many more examples of reinvestment of property tax dollars into Ward 14 in the years to come. I will work to ensure future projects are delivered more efficiently." The facility is being built on the site of the existing Walden Temporary Fire Station and will help meet the long-term service needs of southeast Calgary. The temporary fire station has served the area since 2020 and will remain fully operational during construction, ensuring uninterrupted emergency response while the new permanent station is built. Once the permanent facility becomes operational, the temporary station will be removed. "This new station will strengthen our ability to provide timely emergency response in Calgary's south and ensure firefighters have the facilities, equipment and resources they need to serve the community effectively," says Steve Dongworth, Fire Chief, Calgary Fire Department. "As these communities continue to grow, investments in emergency services help us maintain the high standard of service Calgarians expect." The new full-service Library will include collections, children's spaces, technology, meeting rooms and programming space in Calgary's growing southeast, where demand for Library service continues to increase. “Walden Fire Station and Library brings long-needed, important civic infrastructure to a community who will now have a place to gather and connect together,” says Sarah Meilleur, CEO, Calgary Public Library. “Calgary Public Library and Calgary Fire have worked together for many years to support communities through programming, learning opportunities and public safety education. Walden is the first location where that partnership will be reflected in the building itself, bringing emergency services and lifelong learning together in one community hub.” About the Walden Fire Station and Library The Walden Fire Station and Library will be Calgary's first combined fire station and public library, bringing together two important community services in one location. Building on a long-standing partnership between Calgary Fire and Calgary Public Library, the facility will support fast and reliable emergency services while providing a welcoming place to read, learn and gather for residents of Walden, Legacy, Chaparral, Wolf Willow and surrounding communities. It will include: · A 15,000-square-foot, two-bay permanent fire station. · A 11,000-square-foot Calgary Public Library location. · Parking for staff and the public. For project updates and more information, visit the Walden Fire Station and Library project webpage or contact the project team at Walden@calgary.ca.

title: Largest missing-person response in CPS history leads to recommendations for future critical incidents
summary: Today, we are publicly releasing the key themes from our operational and investigative review of the search for 11-year-old Parker. The review was undertaken internally to identify lessons learned, recognize what worked well and recommend practical improvements for future missing-person investigations, major searches and other prolonged critical incidents. It does not assess the performance of individual employees or partners, nor does it reinvestigate the circumstances of Parker's disappearance. The search for Parker became the largest missing-person response in CPS history, involving a sustained, multi-agency operation, extensive community participation and significant investigative, search, technological and communications resources. The review found that members, partner agencies, volunteers and community members demonstrated extraordinary commitment throughout the response while also identifying opportunities to strengthen organizational systems and processes for future incidents. The review found a number of significant strengths across the response, including: Investigation-led search management Public awareness and community engagement Technology and digital evidence capabilities Strong partnerships and interagency collaboration The professionalism, compassion and adaptability demonstrated by members and partners throughout the response The review also identified opportunities to strengthen organizational systems related to: Scalable resourcing and operational sustainability Command integration and incident management Tip, task and canvass management Public alerting and partnership frameworks Technology readiness and scalability Member wellness and operational resilience One of the key findings involved the unprecedented volume of information received during the investigation. The response generated approximately 1,000 formal investigative tips, more than 90,000 direct social media messages, thousands of emails and approximately 10 terabytes of CCTV footage. The review found that while this information provided significant investigative value, existing systems were not designed to easily manage information at that scale during a prolonged critical incident. The review found that additional capacity and stronger organizational systems would have helped the CPS receive, assess, assign and track the extraordinary volume of information more efficiently. It does not conclude that different resources, systems or processes would have changed the outcome. Rather, it identifies opportunities to improve future responses through better coordination, continuity, information management and operational planning. The review also acknowledges the provincial review on alerting is underway and the recent findings released by The City related to the initial 9-1-1 response. The CPS recognizes and respects The City's review process and responsibilities. The CPS review examined the police response, including investigations, search operations, public engagement, communications, technology and partnerships. It identifies Calgary 9-1-1 as an essential partner in future policy development, training, information sharing, tip management and major incident planning. Formal recommendations were identified across investigations, search management, incident command, strategic communications, partnerships and public alerting, tip management, technology and member wellness. These recommendations will inform future policy development, training, exercises, technology investments and operational planning. We recognize that renewed discussion of this case may be difficult for Parker's family, members involved in the response and many others in our community. The release of these key themes is intended to support transparency, accountability and continuous improvement while honouring the collective effort invested in the search for Parker. The Calgary Police Service Victim Assistance Support Team (VAST) is a free service that provides support, resources and information to victims of crime and tragedy. For anyone who needs support, VAST can be reached at 403-428-8398 or toll-free at 1-888-327-7828. More information is available at https://www.calgary.ca/cps/community-programs-and-resources/victims-of-crime/victim-assistance-support-team.html Key themes from the review: Extraordinary commitment from members and partners Members worked prolonged hours, volunteered outside their regular duties and remained focused on locating Parker and supporting his family. The review found that investigators, search managers, operational commanders, support staff and partners demonstrated extraordinary professionalism and determination. More than 800 searcher deployments were contributed during the response, with personnel from across the CPS and numerous partner agencies stepping in to support investigative, search, operational and community engagement efforts. The review repeatedly notes that many successes were achieved because of the commitment and adaptability of people across the organization. Scalable resourcing and operational sustainability The response tested the CPS' ability to sustain staffing, preserve knowledge, relieve personnel and coordinate resources over an extended period. As the investigation grew more complex, maintaining continuity became increasingly important. The review found that key personnel developed extensive knowledge that was difficult to transfer between shifts or personnel rotations and that many support functions were scaled up through individual initiative rather than formal surge plans. The review recommends a more formal and scalable approach to investigative staffing, relief planning, knowledge transfer, resource generation and operational continuity during prolonged critical incidents. Investigation-led search management The review found that search operations were most effective when guided by current investigative information and when search findings were continuously fed back into the investigation. Search managers, investigators, geomatics specialists and partner agencies worked together to adjust priorities as new information emerged, rather than relying solely on traditional search practices. The review reinforces the importance of maintaining a close connection between investigative and search functions and recommends updates to policy, training, documentation and governance to align with current standards and emerging best practices. Clearer command integration As the response evolved, additional planning, logistics and resource coordination functions were introduced to support the investigation and search effort. The review found that these functions provided significant value, but that roles, responsibilities and activation thresholds were not always clearly understood across all groups involved in the response. It recommends greater clarity around how investigators, search management, the Real Time Operations Centre, Major Events and Emergency Management and incident-management functions work together during prolonged critical incidents, supported by policy updates, training and exercises. Communications as an operational function The review found that communications became much more than a public information function. Media engagement, public appeals, social media content, community outreach and family communications directly influenced investigative outcomes by generating leads, encouraging evidence submissions, directing public action and countering misinformation. Communications professionals also managed significant volumes of public engagement throughout the response. As a result, the review recommends embedding Strategic Communications further within major-incident command structures and ensuring communications capacity is considered when planning for large-scale public engagement campaigns. Partnerships and public alerting The response relied heavily on partnerships with government agencies, search-and-rescue organizations, community partners, the Missing Children Society of Canada and members of the public. Public awareness efforts, including the Alberta Emergency Alert, MCSC Rescu platform, extensive media coverage and social media outreach, helped expand awareness of Parker's disappearance far beyond Calgary. The review found these partnerships and alerting tools generated significant public participation and investigative information, while also creating substantial operational demands. It recommends clearer alerting frameworks, a more formalized relationship with MCSC and continued CPS involvement in discussions around future alerting tools for vulnerable missing persons. Centralized tip, task and canvass management The review found that one of the greatest challenges was not generating information, but managing the unprecedented volume of information received. Approximately 1,000 formal investigative tips, more than 90,000 direct social media messages, thousands of emails and significant volumes of digital evidence were received through multiple intake channels. Investigators often had to reconcile duplicate information, determine ownership and verify follow-up across separate systems. The review recommends a centralized tip-management system, consolidated canvass tracking, clear ownership and stronger information-sharing standards to improve coordination and reduce duplication during future major incidents. Technology as a core operational capability Technology played a critical role throughout the response and significantly expanded what was operationally possible. Mapping tools, video analytics software, drones, digital evidence platforms and public evidence-submission tools supported evidence collection, information sharing, search coordination and investigative decision-making. However, the review found that supporting infrastructure, server capacity, licensing models, technical support and trained-user availability were strained by the scale of demand. It recommends additional investment in technology readiness, training and scalability to support future major incidents. Member wellness The review recognizes member wellness as an operational-readiness issue rather than solely an individual responsibility. The sustained nature of the response exposed members to long hours, high workloads, emotionally difficult circumstances and intense public scrutiny. While wellness supports were made available, the review found that future major incidents would benefit from wellness being formally integrated into planning, operations and demobilization processes from the outset. Recommendations include proactive outreach, clear wellness activation processes and stronger coordination between operational and wellness teams during prolonged critical incidents. title: Water main repairs impacting traffic on 14th Street S.W. - Boil Water Advisory still in effect.
summary: On Friday, October 16, City crews began repairs on a water main that supports the community of Eagle Ridge and Heritage Park. During the repairs, they experienced an unanticipated depressurization of the pipe and could not guarantee the water quality. As a precaution, Alberta Health Services ordered a Boil Water Advisory. This issue is not related to the Bearspaw South Feeder Main, nor is it impacting Rockyview General Hospital. To complete repairs, two northbound and two southbound lanes on 14th Street S.W. between 75 Avenue S.W. and Heritage Drive. S.W. will be closed until further notice, leaving one lane open in each direction. Depending on the condition of the pipe we may need to adjust the lane closures to complete the repair. This is a challenging repair and will take some time to complete. Significant traffic delays are likely. Please use alternative routes if possible and follow all signage and detours. All residents within the affected area are advised to bring all tap water to a rolling boil for one full minute prior to any consumption, including: Drinking, including coffee and tea Cooking Brushing teeth Cleaning raw foods Preparing infant formula or juices Making ice, etc. In-home water filters are not sufficient and water in them must still be boiled before use. You may instead choose to purchase bottled water for consumption for the duration of this advisory. Water wagons are being provided, and their location will be available on calgary.ca/boilwater . When cleaning: If you are not using a dishwasher, water used for cleaning surfaces or dishes should be boiled. Water used for bathing and laundry does not require boiling. For businesses: Food Service Establishments, Care Providers and Personal Service facilities should contact Environmental Public Health at 1-833-476-4743 for direction. This advisory will remain in effect until further notice. Affected residents will be contacted directly when the advisory is lifted and updates will be available on calgary.ca/boilwater . The City of Calgary is working closely with Alberta Environment and Protected Areas and Alberta Health Services to resolve the water quality concerns. For health-related questions and further information about boil water procedures, please contact Health Link at 811 or visit myhealth.alberta.ca/Alberta/Pages/Boil-water-advisory-how-to-use-water-safely.aspx

title: Calgary Fire Department highlights multi-agency response to fatal transit bus collision and fire
summary: At approximately 1:10 p.m. on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026, Calgary Fire Department (CFD) crews were dispatched to the 800 block of Saddletowne Circle N.E., near the intersection of 80 Avenue N.E., for a multi-vehicle collision involving two Calgary Transit buses. Upon arrival, firefighters encountered several severely damaged vehicles, multiple patients with varying degrees of injury, and one transit bus driver trapped inside their vehicle. A second transit bus was involved in a significant fire, with flames and heavy smoke visible from the vehicle. Recognizing the complexity and severity of the incident, firefighters immediately stretched hose lines and began knocking down the fire while requesting additional resources. A mass casualty incident was subsequently declared. As Calgary Police Service (CPS) officers and Emergency Health Services (EHS) personnel arrived on scene, firefighters worked simultaneously to extinguish the bus fire, stabilize the trapped driver and support patient care operations. Calgary Fire Department established the Unified Command Post, providing a central location for incident command and coordination between CFD, CPS, EHS, Calgary Transit and other supporting agencies throughout the response. The CFD Technical Rescue Team was deployed to support the advanced extrication of the trapped bus driver. Working in close coordination with EHS personnel, technical rescue firefighters safely and efficiently removed the driver from the vehicle and transferred them to awaiting medical care. Following extinguishment of the fire, CFD Hazardous Materials specialists worked alongside Calgary Transit personnel to assess the compressed natural gas (CNG) system and confirm it had been safely vented, eliminating any ongoing risk to responders or the public. During suppression and search operations related to the bus fire, firefighters located three deceased persons. Calgary Police Service subsequently confirmed the three individuals were passengers aboard the second transit bus who died following the collision and subsequent fire. This was an exceptionally challenging incident for all responding personnel. Firefighters arrived to find multiple injured patients, a trapped bus driver and a transit bus on fire, requiring simultaneous rescue, firefighting and patient care operations. Throughout the incident, responders from CFD, Calgary Police Service, Emergency Health Services, Calgary Transit and 9-1-1 communications worked together under difficult circumstances to provide the highest level of service possible. CFD acknowledges the professionalism, teamwork and dedication demonstrated by all personnel involved in this tragic event. CFD Fire Investigators attended the scene and have begun investigating the origin and cause of the bus fire. Their investigation is proceeding concurrently with the collision investigation being conducted by Calgary Police Service and the death investigation being conducted by the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner. -30-

title: Three deceased following multi-vehicle collision
summary: Update: The third deceased passenger has since been identified, and their next of kin have been notified. Our Traffic Section continues to investigate a multi-vehicle collision in northeast Calgary that resulted in three fatalities and left one person with life-altering injuries. At approximately 1:10 p.m., on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026, a City of Calgary transit bus was travelling northbound in the 800 block of Saddletowne Circle N.E., approaching the intersection of 80 Avenue N.E. It is believed the bus struck a truck travelling in the same direction. The truck entered an adjacent lane, where it sideswiped a SUV before continuing forward and striking the rear of a box truck. The bus continued northbound and struck the rear of a sedan, pushing the vehicle through the intersection. The sedan then travelled toward Saddletowne Circle N.E., where it struck a truck. Both vehicles eventually came to rest. The bus continued northbound and struck the rear of a second City of Calgary transit bus. Both buses travelled a short distance following the collision before coming to a stop. During the collision, the natural-gas tanks on the second bus ignited. The second bus continued forward before striking a sedan. Within seconds, the fire intensified resulting in an explosion and significant fire inside the bus. Three passengers on the second bus were found deceased. Two have since been identified and their next of kin have been notified. Efforts to identify the third individual remain ongoing. The driver of the second bus was able to exit the vehicle. The driver of the first bus was transported to hospital with life-altering injuries. The remaining drivers involved in the collision were either uninjured or sustained minor injuries. As a result of the multi-vehicle collision, 16 people sustained minor injuries, including an officer who is now recovering at home. At this time, it is too early to determine whether impairment, speed or distraction contributed to the collision. All possible factors remain under investigation. title: Water restrictions take effect Nov. 4 as Bearspaw South Feeder Main enters final steps of construction
summary: Calgary is one step closer to a stronger and more reliable water system as crews prepare to connect the new Bearspaw South Feeder Main into the existing water system, beginning November 4. While this work is underway, city-wide Stage 4 outdoor water restrictions and indoor water conservation will be needed for approximately four weeks to reduce demand while the water supply is limited. This connection marks one of the final steps of installation for the new feeder main. Once connected, crews will begin the final commissioning work required to bring the new pipe into service by the end of this year. "The November connection is a significant phase of the project because it is when the new feeder main will be integrated into Calgary's existing water system," said Michael Thompson, Chief Operating Officer - Water. "Over the past several months, our focus has been on advancing construction while securing the specialized materials needed to complete this work. With the majority of those materials now on-site in Calgary and the rest of the materials scheduled to arrive on time, we're positioned to move into this final phase and deliver on a key investment in Calgary's water infrastructure that will help reduce the risk of future major disruptions." Water restrictions required during connection work To safely complete the connection of the new pipe, the existing Bearspaw South Feeder Main must be temporarily shut down. During this period, the amount of water that can be distributed across the city will be significantly reduced to 500 million litres a day. We need to stay below this number and ensure we have sufficient water for everyone, including firefighting, if needed. As a result, city-wide Stage 4 outdoor water restrictions and indoor water conservation measures will be required beginning Nov. 4 for approximately four weeks. No outdoor water use will be permitted during this time and we're asking all Calgarians and our neighbours in Airdrie, Chestermere, Strathmore and Tsuut'ina Nation to save water indoors by taking the following actions: Run dishwashers and laundry only when full. Flush toilets only when needed. Take shorter showers. Aim for three minutes. "We know Calgarians have already done a tremendous job reducing water use when needed," said Thompson. "The actions people take during this period will help us complete this work safely and successfully while protecting water services across the city.” Once the new feeder main has been connected, crews will focus on preparing the new line for service. This includes disinfecting the pipe, filling it with water and completing the water quality testing required before the new feeder main can be brought into operation. This process will take approximately two to three weeks. The project remains on track for the new feeder main to be fully operational by the end of the year.

title: Operation Silent Night helps lower vehicle noise levels on 17 Avenue S.W.
summary: Noise monitoring data shows measurable reduction in loud vehicle activity during targeted enforcement initiative A data-driven approach to reducing excessive vehicle noise is delivering results on one of Calgary's busiest corridors. Noise monitoring data collected during Operation Silent Night shows measurable improvements in sound levels and a reduction in loud vehicle activity along 17 Avenue S.W., an area identified as Calgary's highest-priority vehicle noise hot spot. To evaluate the impact of the initiative, The City analyzed data from a noise monitor near Tomkins Park and compared results from the August 2026 enforcement period with the same period in 2025. The findings show a significant reduction in loud vehicle events and overall noise levels. During enforcement hours, loud vehicle events decreased from 357 events in 2025 to 267 events in 2026, a reduction of 25.2 per cent. Across the full analysis period, loud vehicle events decreased from 801 to 715, a reduction of 10.7 per cent. Average sound levels during enforcement hours also fell from 71.18 dBA to 68.80 dBA, a decrease of 2.38 decibels. “The results show that when drivers understand the rules and see a visible enforcement presence, we can make a meaningful difference in reducing excessive vehicle noise and improving the quality of life for residents and businesses,” said Brad Johnson, Inspector and head of the Traffic Safety Team. The strongest reductions were observed during active enforcement periods, suggesting a positive impact from increased awareness and officer presence. While factors such as weather, traffic volumes and special events can influence sound levels, the monitoring data indicates a clear improvement during the operation period. The results also highlight the value of Calgary's citywide noise-monitoring network. The monitors provide objective information about loud vehicle activity, helping The City identify noise hot spots, understand trends and evaluate the effectiveness of initiatives aimed at improving community livability. Operation Silent Night demonstrates how data, technology and targeted enforcement can work together to reduce excessive vehicle noise and support quieter, more enjoyable public spaces for residents, businesses and visitors. -30-
